2.text: This is the surest sign by which to recognize their particular properties.

3.text: The other deceased persons are good.”

4.text: The idea of persons doubly dead exists also among other primitive

5.text: tribes.¹ “The Greenlanders pitied the poor souls who must pass in storm the

9.text: The distinction between the good and bad classes of deceased persons

10.text: drawn by my Chukchee informers does not correspond, however, to other

11.text: conceptions, and only accentuates the contradictory state of ideas that exists

12.text: about this matter. The idea of deceased people being harmful is much more

13.text: common than the belief in the protecting powers of deceased ancestors.³
13.note: line ends with superscript footnote marker 3, no quotation mark on the raster; mz draft appended a stray straight quote instead of the marker

14.text: Fear of the dead and the idea of the necessity of taking precautionary

15.text: measures against their return are so deeply implanted in the Chukchee mind

16.text: that they appear even in the children’s plays. In the Maritime villages I

17.text: saw young boys amusing themselves among the ruins of underground houses

18.text: with a peculiar play of this kind. One boy would pretend to be dead.

19.text: Then his companions would bind him up with thong, and carry him away

20.text: to the place of pretended funeral. After a while he would turn to a keˊlᴇ,
20.as_typed: to the place of pretended funeral. After a while he would turn to a {ke'le_},

21.text: and come back to the house with frightful cries and grimaces. One of the

22.text: boys would act as a shaman, and beat the imaginary drum. Then the keˊlᴇ
22.note: confirmed at 4x: a stress mark is present between e and l (mz draft dropped it, reading 'ke lE')
22.as_typed: boys would act as a shaman, and beat the imaginary drum. Then the {ke'le_}

23.text: would act like a shamanistic spirit, and answer to the songs and calls of the

25.text: Especially harmful is the dead body, even the merest fragments of it,

26.text: which, as said before, are used in preparing the much-dreaded “spells.” A

27.text: man who, walking alone in the country, suddenly meets a corpse lying in the

28.text: open, incurs great danger. If he turns back and tries to retrace his steps,

29.text: the corpse will follow, and soon will pass ahead of him, barring his way.

30.text: From that time he will have hardly a chance of escape, and finally the dead

31.text: one will act on him as a keˊlᴇ of Iuˊmetun, throwing him into the much-
31.as_typed: one will act on him as a {ke'le_} of {Iu'metun}, throwing him into the much-

32.text: dreaded fits and convulsions.⁴ This belief evidently arises from the fact

33.text: that Iuˊmetun is also supposed to live in the open country, where he
33.as_typed: that {Iu'metun} is also supposed to live in the open country, where he

34.text: watches the victims occasionally passing by, and then pursues them, following

35.text: leisurely but very obstinately behind. Nevertheless, even in the matter of
